query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy is derived from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi and is intended to retain a favorable strength–ductility balance in its solidified solid-solution state, but its dynamic behavior across different temperatures and strain rates lacks a theoretical explanation. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could account for this behavior, and what controlled comparison within that regime would distinguish it? Specify predictions relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and a falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Under dynamic loading, the Co‐free FeNiCrMn alloy forms ultra‐nanocrystalline/amorphous boundary layers that locally weaken shear resistance, thereby enabling enhanced ductility without a severe loss in strength. This dynamic amorphization mechanism activates more readily in the absence of Co, compared to the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: Solid-solution single-phase Co‐free FeNiCrMn alloy produced by removing Co from the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi composition
generation.intervention: Systematically vary strain rate and temperature in deformation/wear tests under inert (non-oxidizing) conditions to provoke the grain boundary transformation.
generation.conditions: Mechanical tests conducted across a range of strain rates (from quasi‐static to high) and temperatures (ambient to moderately elevated) in environments where oxidation is suppressed; microstructure is initially a single-phase solid solution without significant precipitates.
generation.structural_mediator: Dynamic formation of ultra‐nanocrystalline or amorphous grain boundary layers
generation.mechanism: Under dynamic stress conditions, local energy concentration at grain boundaries induces a transformation (dynamic amorphization) which forms ultra‐fine, lubricious layers at interfaces. This process reduces local shear strength, assisting in grain boundary sliding or recrystallization that improves ductility while retaining a reasonable strength level. The removal of Co is hypothesized to destabilize the traditional grain-boundary structure, making this transformation more favorable compared to the baseline alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the Co-containing equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloy, the Co‐free FeNiCrMn alloy is expected to show a measurable drop in yield strength at high strain rates or elevated temperatures combined with improved ductility, as evidenced by lower friction coefficients and observational signs of ultra‐nanocrystalline (or amorphized) grain boundary layers after deformation.
generation.baseline: Behavior of the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloy under identical strain rate and temperature testing conditions
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to conditions where the material remains a single-phase solid solution (i.e., minimal precipitation effects) and in inert environments (to avoid oxidation effects). Outside these ranges (e.g., if significant precipitation occurs or in oxidizing environments), other mechanisms may dominate the behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The precise onset (in terms of strain rate and temperature) for dynamic amorphization and the quantification of its effects on strength and ductility remain to be defined, as do the potential interactions with other deformation mechanisms.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a series of uniaxial tensile and wear tests on both Co‐free FeNiCrMn and equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloys, varying the strain rate and temperature in an inert atmosphere. Use high-resolution electron microscopy (e.g., TEM/STEM) to study grain boundary structure before and after deformation, and measure friction coefficients and stress–strain responses during testing.
measurements: Grain boundary structure and grain size distributions via TEM/STEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, under high strain rate or elevated temperature conditions, the Co‐free FeNiCrMn alloy fails to exhibit a significant increase in ultra‐nanocrystalline or amorphous grain boundary layers (relative to the baseline) and does not display the predicted reduction in yield strength with concomitant retention or improvement of ductility, then this dynamic amorphization hypothesis must be rejected.

cited_evidence.text:
Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
